relevant_pages.reason: States that some firms present information in misleading or hard‑to‑understand ways, directly framing expectations for fair, clear consumer communications
Introduces Consumer Principle and cross‑cutting rules (act in good faith, avoid foreseeable harm, support customer objectives) that apply to how marketing and consumer communications are framed
Outcomes include consumers being equipped with the right information to make effective, timely and properly informed decisions, an overarching expectation applicable to communication content
Specifies that consumers must be equipped with the right information to make effective, timely and properly informed decisions about products and services, a checkable communications standard
mentions firms changing communications standards for in-scope vs out-of-scope customers
discusses potentially developing different communications for retail and non-retail customer groups
defines which firms preparing and approving communications to retail customers are subject to the Duty
sets scoping rule that products marketed and approved only to non-retail customers are outside Duty, affecting which communications are governed
states that for regulated buy-to-let mortgages only financial promotion rules and relevant communications aspects of the Duty apply
introduces the high-level Consumer Principle that firms must act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, which marketing communications could breach
confirms final wording of the Consumer Principle and explains its outcomes focus beyond Principles 6 and 7, applicable to how firms communicate with consumers
discusses consumers needing information and support to make informed decisions, implying expectations on the content and quality of communications
clarifies reasonable, proportionate application of the Duty based on product risk and customer characteristics, framing how stringent marketing and disclosure communications must be
Links TCF outcomes and existing Principle 6/7 guidance to new Principle 12 standards applicable to communications
Sets out cross‑cutting rules (good faith, avoiding foreseeable harm, supporting financial objectives) that marketing texts must not breach
Explains assessing customers’ reasonable expectations and gives stage‑of‑relationship examples relevant to how firms communicate
States that firms must consider consumers’ limited experience and behavioural biases and references consumer understanding rules for communications
Requires firms to create an environment where consumers can act in their own interests, considering behavioural biases and vulnerability, which applies to communications
Discusses design, approval, marketing and ongoing management of products/services, making marketing part of governance for good outcomes
Touches on financial exclusion and suggests (though not mandates) inclusive‑design principles affecting how products and related communications meet vulnerable customers’ needs
Mentions ceasing marketing and the role of additional disclosure to address identified harms, directly affecting communication content and use
Gives expectations on complexity of visible product features and warns that increased disclosure can cause information overload, guiding how information is presented in communications
Introduces fair‑value outcome and notes need to consider non‑monetary costs/benefits and practices like price walking, which may be evidenced in pricing claims within marketing materials
Sets expectations that firms’ communications must give consumers needed information at the right time and in a way they can understand

States that firms must ensure explanations are likely to be understood and equip customers to make effective, timely and properly informed decisions, and applies outcome to all communications including online and verbal
Clarifies firms can and should support consumer understanding within advice/guidance and data‑protection constraints, discussing what non‑marketing and marketing messages may contain
Requires communications to be understandable by intended recipients, including vulnerable customers, and gives examples of tailoring and prominence in communications
Requires tailoring communications on a one‑to‑one basis where appropriate, which can be checked from individual communication content

Describes outcome that communications give needed information at the right time in an understandable way, and specifies key content (actions, consequences, features, costs, risks, access to support) that consumers must be able to identify and understand
mentions customer service and support expectations that can shape how communications describe support and channels offered
sets obligations that limited-channel products must clearly communicate their support channels and limitations before sale
states that unclear or confusing digital customer journeys will not meet standards, impacting how online communications and journeys must be presented
expects firms, when declining access to a product or service, to provide information/signposting to help customers meet financial objectives, affecting communication content
clarifies firms must consider diverse needs in how they support and communicate with customers, including those with characteristics of vulnerability
mentions reviewing the most significant communications as part of risk‑based implementation, which scopes obligations about communications content
expects firms to prioritise review of the most significant communications, indirectly scoping marketing/communication obligations under the Duty
states overarching Consumer Duty standard of care and focus on delivering good outcomes that marketing communications themselves must not undermine
discusses consumers being put in a position to make informed decisions, implying expectations on how information and communications enable decision‑making, which can be checked in marketing texts
Defines ‘non-retail financial instrument’ partly via required content and targeting of marketing materials and promotional communications
Continues definition of ‘non-retail financial instrument’ including conditions on marketing materials and associated promotional communications
Defines ‘retail market business’ partly by excluding certain offers and associated promotional communications, scoping which communications rules apply
Glossary definition of ‘financial promotion rules’ explicitly links PRIN principles and rules to financial promotions, directly scoping communication content obligations
defines ‘regulated market’ with specific linkage to Principle 12, helping scope where consumer-duty communication rules apply
defines ‘retail customer’ and ‘manufacture’/‘manufacturer’ for PRIN, directly scoping which customers and products communication obligations apply
sets out Principles 7 and 12 including ‘clear, fair and not misleading’ and ‘good outcomes’ which are overarching standards marketing communications must meet
explains that Principle 12 imposes a higher standard than Principles 6 and 7 and applies to retail market business, framing how communications must achieve good customer outcomes
introduces cross‑cutting obligations under Principle 12 including acting in good faith and avoiding exploiting emotions or behavioural biases, which a communication itself could breach
gives examples of not acting in good faith including how information is presented and manipulating or exploiting customers’ emotions or behavioural biases to create product demand
sets obligation to avoid causing foreseeable harm and requires that product design, terms, marketing, sale and support avoid foreseeable harm and not exploit behavioural biases
continues guidance on avoiding foreseeable harm, including ensuring customers do not face unreasonable barriers when they want to switch or complain, which can be implemented via communications

obligation to enable and support customers to pursue financial objectives, including ensuring product design, terms, marketing, sale and support meet customer objectives and providing necessary information and support
clarifies that cross‑cutting obligations apply at all stages of the customer journey and require proactive and reactive conduct, including via ongoing communications
states that cross-cutting obligations apply when designing communications and at target-market level, linking Principle 12 to expectations that can govern marketing conduct
defines ‘marketing’ and ‘distributing’ for existing products, scoping how marketing activity is covered under these rules
requires value assessments before a product is marketed or distributed and links marketing of existing/closed products to these obligations, which can condition marketing claims
defines non-financial costs including provision and use of personal data, which can be relevant to disclosures in marketing and customer communications
Defines scope of communications rules and obliges all retail communications to be clear, fair, not misleading, and to support customer understanding and decision-making
Sets detailed content and presentation expectations for communications (plain language, prominence of key information, timely provision, appropriate channels)
Requires tailoring of communications to customer characteristics and sets obligations for one-to-one interactions that can be checked from dialogue/communications
Imposes duties around testing, monitoring, and adapting communications when they do not support good outcomes, partially assessable from the content and framing of marketing/communications

Requires firms to notify other firms about problematic communications in the distribution chain and provide information so it can be communicated to customers, affecting what appears in communications
Customer support rules include requirements on appropriate friction and avoiding unreasonable barriers, some of which can be assessed from wording and structure of customer-facing messages
Further explains what constitutes unreasonable barriers and delays in customer support communications, which can be checked against the wording and framing of such interactions
Sets out overarching standard of a prudent firm including duties around promoting and supporting consumer understanding of complex products, which bears on how communications must be framed
Mentions specific requirements on testing and monitoring of retail customer communications, directly scoping communication-related obligations
Requires firms to explain identified harm to retail customers in a way that is fair, clear and not misleading, which is a checkable standard for remedial communications
Clarifies application of Principle 12 and PRIN 2A, tying them to communication and approval of financial promotions and thus scoping which communications must meet those standards
Scopes Principles including 6,7,12 and PRIN 2A to communication and financial promotion activities relevant to marketing texts
Defines the application of Principle 12 and PRIN 2A to retail market business and distribution chains, which frames when communication-related duties apply
Extends territorial scope of Principle 12 and PRIN 2A to activities with UK retail customers, covering where communication duties bite
Explains interaction and possible disapplication limits of Principle 12 and PRIN 2A, which condition the applicability of communication-content obligations
Introduces Individual Conduct Rule 6 (act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers), an overarching conduct principle that marketing communications themselves could breach

Sets out conduct rules requiring acting in good faith, avoiding foreseeable harm, and supporting customers’ financial objectives—overarching principles checkable against marketing and consumer communications
Links PRIN 2A cross‑cutting and outcome rules to interpretation of Rule 6, clarifying how Consumer Duty outcome expectations apply to conduct including communications
Explains that Rule 6 (good outcomes for retail customers) imposes a higher standard than treating customers fairly, framing expectations that communications must not undermine good consumer outcomes

Describes factors for applying the good outcomes duty, including situations where staff follow scripts or processes when dealing with retail customers, relevant to how scripted communications are designed and used

Clarifies responsibilities of salespersons and customer support staff for influencing outcomes for retail customers, relevant to how their verbal and written communications must align with good outcomes principles
Links Principle 12 and PRIN 2A to product-governance obligations, which scope how product-related communications must support good consumer outcomes
